title: Nebius Confronts Microsoft’s Neocloud Cull With Delivery Receipts
subtitle: A brutal sector selloff tests whether verified capacity protects the landlord of the AI boom.
summary: Microsoft is cutting back its roster of third-party GPU suppliers to focus on vendors that actually deliver working clusters on time. Nebius trades down sharply alongside peers that slipped, even though its filings show all contracted capacity handed over on schedule.

bodyHtml:
Every subscription you pay for eventually gets an audit. You cut the gym pass you stopped using, drop the extra streaming tier, and keep only the services that actually work when you hit play. Microsoft is now running the exact same ruthless math on the companies supplying its artificial intelligence muscle.

Nebius is essentially the commercial landlord of the AI boom. The Amsterdam-based company builds the physical shell and secures high-voltage power agreements. It fills the racks with top-tier Nvidia processors, then rents the computing capacity on long-term leases to tech giants and research labs that cannot pour concrete fast enough to meet demand. Instead of selling software, it sells wired, ready-to-run raw compute by the cluster.

For three years, the market treated any startup with a signed GPU contract like an untouchable winner. That grace period just evaporated.

On Nov. 6, reports revealed that Microsoft is quietly winnowing its massive list of third-party cloud partners down to a handful of core operators. It is letting peripheral agreements lapse and bringing critical capacity under its own roof. The software titan already declined to renew arrangements with Oracle and Nscale, while requested networking overhauls pushed capacity from rival operator IREN into early next year.

That sudden customer discipline sparked a sector-wide panic. Nebius shares tumbled more than 45% over the past month, caught in the identical downdraft that hammered competitors like CoreWeave. The equity now trades more than 55% below its June peak.

Yet grouping Nebius with operators struggling to connect their gear misses what the legal filings show. In a neocloud shakeout, signed paper is just a promise, but plugged-in servers are collateral.

The company holds a $17.39 billion multi-year agreement with Microsoft, backed by an immediate $6.958 billion upfront cash prepayment covering 40% of the total commitment. Rivals saw timelines slip, and Nscale's planned UK site fell through over electricity access. Nebius confirmed in August that it had delivered every scheduled capacity tranche from its New Jersey campus, two of them in the prior month.

There is also a multi-billion-dollar framework with Meta that scales on Nvidia’s upcoming architecture. Nebius closed the first half of the year holding nearly $37.5 billion in contracted revenue backlog.

Why this matters to the broader tech landscape comes down to the marginal gigawatt. Hyperscalers like Microsoft are burning through more than $45 billion a quarter on physical assets, but the electrical grid cannot move at the speed of software. Specialized operators serve as the relief valve when internal data-center construction runs behind schedule.

When the primary customer consolidates that supplier base, incremental computing supply concentrates into fewer hands, ensuring smaller, sub-scale operators get squeezed out of the buildout entirely.

For the stock to stage a lasting recovery, the market needs concrete proof that the business model can fund its own staggering appetite. Nebius is not just expanding; it is attempting an industrial sprint, with capital expenditures projected at up to $25 billion for the year.

The equity re-rates higher only if prepayments keep funding half to 60% of the hardware bill on most new deals. That is what insulates common shareholders from toxic dilution and high-cost borrowing. When prepayments arrive like clockwork, Nebius operates as an asset-backed consolidator; if they dry up, the company is just another highly leveraged debtor building depreciating compute clusters.

The short case writes itself around that exact balance sheet vulnerability. Microsoft accounts for roughly 46% of the company's contracted revenue backlog, giving one counterparty enormous leverage over its fate. The contract explicitly allows Microsoft to cancel individual capacity tranches if delivery schedules slip or systems fail availability standards.

Meanwhile, trailing twelve-month free cash flow sits at negative $5.88 billion, and interest expenses exploded twenty-five-fold over the past year. The company also took on a $3.5 billion short-term bank facility alongside convertible notes that pay cash coupons of just 1% to 3% but cost roughly 5% all-in once the discount is amortized. To make matters worse, top insiders have unloaded roughly $158 million in shares since August. One executive sale topped $90 million just weeks before the tech sector wobbled.

What we are watching next is the third-quarter earnings report scheduled for Nov. 12, before the opening bell. Investors need two specific checkpoints. The first is whether contracted backlog holds firm above $37 billion without canceled commitments. The second is whether deferred revenue confirms that customer cash advances are still absorbing the construction bill.

Until those numbers hit the tape, the market is pricing a verified builder as if its primary tenant already walked out the door.
